Comparing Two Groups with prolfqua

Witold E. Wolski

2026-11-02

Source: vignettes/Comparing2Groups.Rmd
Comparing2Groups.Rmd

Purpose

This vignette demonstrates how two conditions, e.g., treatment vs. control, can be compared and the differences statistically tested. We use simulated protein abundances of an LFQ experiment with two treatment groups (A, B) and a control group (Ctrl). After first examining the data using QC plots and then normalizing the data, we compare each treatment group with the control. The output of the comparison is the difference in the mean intensities for quantified proteins (log2 fold-change) in each group, along with statistical parameters such as degrees of freedom, standard errors, p-value and the FDR.

Simulated protein abundances 

library(prolfqua)

sim_lfq_data_protein_config() simulates protein abundances in long format, one row per protein and sample, and returns them together with a matching AnalysisConfiguration. To read your own data, see the article Importing your data.

xx <- prolfqua::sim_lfq_data_protein_config(Nprot = 100, weight_missing = 0.5)
xx

Create the LFQData class instance and remove zero or very small intensities, which most quantification software reports for missing values.

lfqdata <- prolfqua::LFQData$new(xx$data, xx$config)
lfqdata$remove_small_intensities()
lfqdata$factors()
## # A tibble: 12 × 3
##    sample  sampleName group_
##    <chr>   <chr>      <chr> 
##  1 A_V1    A_V1       A     
##  2 A_V2    A_V2       A     
##  3 A_V3    A_V3       A     
##  4 A_V4    A_V4       A

##  6 B_V2    B_V2       B     
##  7 B_V3    B_V3       B     
##  8 B_V4    B_V4       B     
##  9 Ctrl_V1 Ctrl_V1    Ctrl  
## 10 Ctrl_V2 Ctrl_V2    Ctrl  
## 11 Ctrl_V3 Ctrl_V3    Ctrl  
## 12 Ctrl_V4 Ctrl_V4    Ctrl

Visualization of not normalized data

After this first setting up of the analysis we show now how to normalize the proteins and the effect of normalization. Furthermore we use some functions to visualize the missing values in our data.

lfqplotter <- lfqdata$get_Plotter()
density_nn <- lfqplotter$intensity_distribution_density()

Visualization of missing data 

lfqplotter$na_heatmap()

Heatmap of missing protein intensities, black - missing, white - present 

lfqdata$get_Summariser()$plot_missingness_per_group()

# of proteins with 0,1,…N missing values 

lfqplotter$missigness_histogram()

Intensity distribution of proteins depending on # of missing values

Computing standard deviations, mean and CV.

Other important statistics such as coefficient of variation, means and standard deviations can be easily calculated using the get_Stats function and visualized with a violin plot.

stats <- lfqdata$get_Stats()
stats$violin()

Violin plots of CVs in the different groups and among all groups 

prolfqua::table_facade( stats$stats_quantiles()$wide, paste0("quantile of ",stats$stat ))

Normalize protein intensities and show diagnostic plots

We normalize the data by log⁡2\log_2 transforming and then z−scalingz-scaling.

lt <- lfqdata$get_Transformer()
transformed <- lt$log2()$robscale()$lfq
transformed$is_transformed()
## [1] TRUE
pl <- transformed$get_Plotter()
density_norm <- pl$intensity_distribution_density()
gridExtra::grid.arrange(density_nn, density_norm)

Distribution of intensities before and after normalization. 

pl$pairs_smooth()

Scatterplot matrix 

## NULL
p <- pl$heatmap_cor()
p

Heatmap, Rows - proteins, Columns - samples

Fit the model and compute contrasts

We compare each treatment group with the control. build_contrast_analysis() fits one model per protein and computes the contrasts in one call. We use the method lm_impute: a linear model per protein, with the protein variances moderated by the empirical Bayes method so that proteins with few observations borrow strength from all proteins. Proteins without observations in one group are refitted with the missing values set to the limit of detection (LOD). The article Filling the gaps uses these models to complete the data for heatmaps and PCA. The vignette All modelling methods at a glance lists the other methods.

contr_spec <- c(
  "AvsC" = "group_A - group_Ctrl",
  "BvsC" = "group_B - group_Ctrl"
)
fa <- build_contrast_analysis(transformed, "~ group_", contr_spec, method = "lm_impute")
contrdf <- fa$get_contrasts()

The column estimate_type tells how each estimate was obtained: observed from the measured intensities, lod_imputed from the refit at the LOD.

dplyr::count(contrdf, contrast, estimate_type)
## # A tibble: 4 × 3
##   contrast estimate_type     n
##   <chr>    <chr>         <int>
## 1 AvsC     lod_imputed       7
## 2 AvsC     observed         93
## 3 BvsC     lod_imputed       7
## 4 BvsC     observed         93
plotter <- fa$get_Plotter()
plotter$volcano()$FDR

Volcano plots of the two contrasts. 

plotter$ma_plot()

MA plot showing the dependency of mean abundance with respect to the difference

The proteins with FDR < 0.1 in at least one contrast:

sig <- dplyr::filter(contrdf, FDR < 0.1)
signif <- transformed$get_copy()
signif$set_data(signif$data_long() |> dplyr::filter(protein_Id %in% sig$protein_Id))
hmSig <- signif$get_Plotter()$heatmap()
hmSig

Heatmap of the proteins with FDR < 0.1 in at least one contrast 

myProteinIDS <- head(unique(contrdf$protein_Id), 3)
dplyr::filter(contrdf, protein_Id %in% myProteinIDS)
## # A tibble: 6 × 16
##   modelName estimate_type protein_Id  contrast    diff avgAbd

fa$get_missing()

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)

After computing contrasts, proteins can be ranked by log2 fold change or t-statistic and subjected to gene set enrichment analysis. The typical workflow is:

  1. Extract UniProt IDs from the contrast results using prolfqua::get_uniprot_id_from_fasta_header()
  2. Map UniProt IDs to Entrez Gene IDs using AnnotationDbi::mapIds() with a species-specific annotation package
  3. Create a named ranked list (statistic values named by gene IDs)
  4. Run GSEA using clusterProfiler::gseGO() or clusterProfiler::gseKEGG()

For details see:

  • clusterProfiler book – comprehensive guide to enrichment analysis in R
  • clusterProfiler Bioconductor page
  • AnnotationDbi – for mapping between gene identifier types

The prolfqua package is described in (Wolski et al. 2023).
